cards.front: What three phases make up an application's execution lifecycle?
cards.back: Compilation, class loading, bytecode execution
cards.extra: javac produces bytecode; the JVM loads classes and then executes them. Almost all of the complexity lives in the third phase.
cards.source: cesarsotovalero.net — The Execution Lifecycle of a Java Application
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: What does the JVM do during the loading phase?
cards.back: Finds the binary form of a class and builds a Class object from it
cards.extra: A ClassLoader locates the .class bytes; defineClass turns them into a java.lang.Class instance.
cards.source: cesarsotovalero.net — The Execution Lifecycle of a Java Application
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: Which class loader loads the Java core classes?
cards.back: The bootstrap class loader
cards.extra: It is built into the JVM and loads from the runtime image (rt.jar on Java 8). Application class loaders load your own classes from the classpath.
cards.source: cesarsotovalero.net — The Execution Lifecycle of a Java Application
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: What are the three steps of linking?
cards.back: Verification, preparation, resolution
cards.extra: Verify the bytecode is well-formed, allocate static storage, then resolve symbolic references — the last step can be deferred.
cards.source: cesarsotovalero.net — The Execution Lifecycle of a Java Application
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.back: That the bytecode is well-formed and obeys the JVM's rules — valid opcodes, branches into instruction starts, correct signatures
cards.extra: This is the safety net that lets the JVM trust bytecode from elsewhere: malformed or hostile class files are rejected before they run.
cards.source: cesarsotovalero.net — The Execution Lifecycle of a Java Application
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.back: Static fields are created and set to default values (0, false, null)
cards.extra: Not to their declared values — that happens later, in initialization. Preparation only allocates and zeroes the storage.
cards.source: cesarsotovalero.net — The Execution Lifecycle of a Java Application
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.back: Lazily — at first actual use, or possibly never
cards.extra: Unlike a C executable, which is fully linked up front. A class that references twenty others may use only two of them.
cards.source: cesarsotovalero.net — The Execution Lifecycle of a Java Application
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: In what order does class initialization run?
cards.back: Superclasses first (up to Object), then static field initializers and static blocks in source order
cards.extra: A static initializer that reads a field declared later sees the default value, because the field's own initializer has not run yet.
cards.source: cesarsotovalero.net — The Execution Lifecycle of a Java Application
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.back: Creating an instance, calling a static method, assigning a static field, or using a non-constant static field
cards.extra: Reflection can also trigger it. Merely declaring a reference to the type does not.
cards.source: cesarsotovalero.net — The Execution Lifecycle of a Java Application
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: Does reading a static final constant trigger class initialization?
cards.back: No — constants are inlined at compile time
cards.extra: The value is copied into the calling class by javac, so the defining class may never load. This is why changing a constant requires recompiling callers.
cards.source: cesarsotovalero.net — The Execution Lifecycle of a Java Application
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: What are the steps of instantiation?
cards.back: Allocate memory on the heap, run the constructor, return the reference
cards.extra: new is explicit, but boxing, string concatenation, string literals and lambdas also create objects without new appearing.
cards.source: cesarsotovalero.net — The Execution Lifecycle of a Java Application
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: Why should you not rely on finalize()?
cards.back: It is not guaranteed to run, and not promptly when it does
cards.extra: It is deprecated for removal. Use try-with-resources or an explicit close for cleanup.
cards.source: cesarsotovalero.net — The Execution Lifecycle of a Java Application
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: When can a loaded class be unloaded?
cards.back: When its defining class loader becomes unreachable and is collected
cards.extra: Classes from the bootstrap loader are never unloaded, so in a normal application class unloading effectively does not happen.
cards.source: cesarsotovalero.net — The Execution Lifecycle of a Java Application
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: How does a Java program terminate normally?
cards.back: When all non-daemon threads finish, or something calls System.exit
cards.extra: Daemon threads do not keep the JVM alive. Runtime.exit halts the VM with a status code.
cards.source: cesarsotovalero.net — The Execution Lifecycle of a Java Application
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.back: At run time, after the program has started — hence "just in time"
cards.extra: The JVM converts bytecode to machine code while the program runs, and can recompile as it learns more.
cards.source: bell-sw.com — Compilation in Java: JIT vs AOT
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.back: A region of code executed often enough to be worth compiling
cards.extra: The JIT profiles the running program and spends its optimisation effort where it will pay off, instead of compiling everything eagerly.
cards.source: bell-sw.com — Compilation in Java: JIT vs AOT
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.back: The period at startup when code still runs interpreted or lightly optimised
cards.extra: It costs latency and extra CPU, and it repeats on every restart — which is why cold starts hurt in containers.
cards.source: bell-sw.com — Compilation in Java: JIT vs AOT
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.back: The client compiler — compiles quickly with simple optimisations
cards.extra: Fast startup, less optimal code. Good for short-lived or UI-facing work.
cards.source: bell-sw.com — Compilation in Java: JIT vs AOT
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.back: The server compiler — profiles first, then applies aggressive optimisations
cards.extra: Slower to warm up, faster at steady state. HotSpot can use both: C1 first, then recompile hot methods with C2.
cards.source: bell-sw.com — Compilation in Java: JIT vs AOT
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.back: Recompiling code during execution as the JIT learns which paths matter
cards.extra: A method that was cold at startup can be recompiled once it becomes hot, or deoptimised if an assumption breaks.
cards.source: bell-sw.com — Compilation in Java: JIT vs AOT
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.back: At build time, before the program ever runs
cards.extra: GraalVM Native Image analyses the bytecode and emits a single native executable for one OS and architecture.
cards.source: bell-sw.com — Compilation in Java: JIT vs AOT
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.back: AOT assumes every class needed at run time is reachable at build time
cards.extra: It lets the compiler strip unreachable code and build a small executable — but anything reached dynamically must be declared or it breaks.
cards.source: bell-sw.com — Compilation in Java: JIT vs AOT
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.back: Near-instant startup, smaller images, no warm-up, smaller attack surface
cards.extra: There is no JVM to start and no interpreter to run the code first, so peak performance arrives immediately.
cards.source: bell-sw.com — Compilation in Java: JIT vs AOT
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: What does AOT give up compared with JIT?
cards.back: Dynamic optimisation — the code is fixed at build time
cards.extra: A native image cannot recompile hot paths, and it supports only a limited set of garbage collectors.
cards.source: bell-sw.com — Compilation in Java: JIT vs AOT
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: Why is reflection a problem for AOT?
cards.back: Reflective access is dynamic, so the closed-world analysis cannot see it
cards.extra: Classes reached only by reflection must be declared in metadata (the Tracing Agent helps produce it), or the native image fails at run time.
cards.source: bell-sw.com — Compilation in Java: JIT vs AOT
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.back: Coordinated Restore at Checkpoint — snapshot a warmed-up JVM and restore it in milliseconds
cards.extra: It keeps the JIT (unlike AOT) while removing repeated warm-up: start once, checkpoint, then restore many instances.
cards.source: bell-sw.com — Compilation in Java: JIT vs AOT
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: Which approach should you choose, JIT or AOT?
cards.back: Match it to the workload: AOT for fast-start, short-lived or scale-to-zero services; JIT for long-running, throughput-heavy ones
cards.extra: The trade is warm-up and footprint against peak performance and dynamic optimisation. Neither wins universally.
cards.source: bell-sw.com — Compilation in Java: JIT vs AOT
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals
